text.en: Ægir may go back to Proto-Germanic *āgwi-jaz, 'the one of the water, water-man', from a stem for 'river' (Gothic aƕa, Old English ēa). In skaldic poetry ægir is also a word for the sea. His other name Gymir is unclear; 'the earthly' and 'the wintry one' have been proposed.

Æsir is the plural of áss 'god' (feminine ásynja, plural ásynjur). The word is shared with Old English ōs and the Gothic Ansis that Jordanes recorded, and lives on in names such as Ansgar and Oswald. Whether it meant the gods in general or one family of gods beside the Vanir is debated.

text.en: Freyja plainly means 'lady, mistress', from Proto-Germanic *frawjōn (Old High German frouwa, German Frau), the female counterpart of Freyr 'lord'. It is thought to have begun as a title that replaced her own, now lost, name.

Freyr means 'lord': from Proto-Germanic *frawjaz, like Gothic frauja and Old English frēa, 'lord, master'. Another view connects it with a word for 'fruitful' (Swedish frö 'seed'), making him 'the fruitful one'; in Sweden his name was Frö.

Frigg comes from Proto-Germanic *Frijjō, from the adjective *frijaz 'free', which in a kin-based society first meant 'one's own, dear'. It is related to Sanskrit priyā 'beloved', to English friend and to the verb 'to love' (*frijōnan); English Friday is Frīg's day.
Fróði was first a byname, the definite form of fróðr 'wise, learned': 'the wise one'.

means.en: perhaps the one who illuminates the world

text.en: The meaning of Heimdallr is obscure; 'the one who illuminates the world' has been proposed, with heimr 'world' as the first part. The name may be connected with Mardöll, one of Freyja's names. His byname Gullintanni means 'the one with the golden teeth'.
Heimdallargaldr means 'Heimdallr's galdr', his incantation or spell-song.

Hel is the same word as the realm she rules: Proto-Germanic *haljō 'concealed place, the underworld', from a verb 'to cover, to hide' (Old English helan), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- 'to conceal'. English hell is the same word, and Latin cēlō 'I hide' a distant relative.
Helblindi means 'Hel-blind'; it is the name of Loki's brother and also one of Óðinn's names.
Helgi is the definite form of an old adjective *heiligr 'happy, lucky', later understood as heilagr 'holy'; Hjǫrvarðsson is 'son of Hjǫrvarðr'.
Helgi is the definite form of an old adjective *heiligr 'happy, lucky'; later it was understood as heilagr 'holy'. Hundingsbani means 'Hundingr's bane'.
Herfjötur means 'war-fetter', 'host-fetter' or 'fetter of the army'.
Herkja is glossed 'noise'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Hermóðr means 'war-spirit': herr 'army, war' and móðr 'spirit, courage'.
Hervarðr joins herr 'army' and varðr 'guardian'; it is the same name as Old English Hereweard (Hereward).
Hildr means 'battle'; it is also a common ending of women's names, as in Brynhildr.
Himinbjörg means 'heaven's castle' or 'heaven-mountain': Heimdallr's home.
Hindarfjall means 'hind mountain': where Brynhildr sleeps.

means.en: perhaps the one returning to health

text.en: Hjúki possibly means 'the one returning to health'.
Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Hleðjolfr as 'shield-wolf'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

means.en: the high seat with a wide view

text.en: Hliðskjálf is taken literally as 'the high seat with an expansive view' (hlið 'opening', skjálf 'bench, shelf'): Óðinn's seat, from which he sees all the worlds.
Hlín is usually explained as 'protector'; Snorri derives it from a verb hleina found only in an obscure proverb.
Hnitbjǫrg can be translated 'colliding rocks', perhaps a mountain that opens and shuts, as in other tales.
Hnoss means 'treasure': Freyja's daughter.
Hoddmímis holt means 'Hoard-Mímir's wood', where Líf and Lífþrasir shelter through Ragnarök.

Hǫðr can be translated 'warrior' or 'battle'. Jan de Vries and Vladimir Orel relate it to Old Norse hǫð 'war, slaughter' and Old English heaðu-deór 'brave in war', from Proto-Germanic *haþuz 'battle'.

means.en: he who throws his hooves about

text.en: Hófvarpnir means 'he who throws his hooves about': the horse of Gná.
Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Hornbori as 'horn-borer'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Hræsvelgr means 'corpse-swallower': the giant in eagle's shape whose wings make the wind.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Hreiðmarr has been glossed 'nest-horse' (hreiðr 'nest', marr 'horse'); the sense is unclear.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Hrímfaxi means 'frost mane': Night's horse, the foam from whose bit falls as dew.
Hrímgerðr is 'frost-Gerðr': hrím 'rime, frost' joined to the name Gerðr.
Hrímnir is glossed 'the one covered with hoarfrost' or 'the sooty one'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Hrímþurs is 'rime-þurs, frost-þurs': hrím 'rime, hoar-frost' and þurs, one of the words for a giant, the same word as Old English þyrs.

means.en: ship with a circle on the stem

text.en: Hringhorni means 'ship with a circle on the stem': Baldr's ship.
Hrólfr comes from earlier *Hróðulfr: hróðr 'fame' and úlfr 'wolf'. It is the same name as Rudolph and Old English Hroðulf.
Hrungnir means 'brawler'.
Hrymr is glossed 'decrepit'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Hugi means 'thought', from hugr: Þjálfi races against thought itself at Útgarða-Loki's.
Huginn is hugr 'thought, mind, mood' with the definite ending, 'the thought'; the word lives on in Icelandic hugur. His fellow raven Muninn is built the same way on a word for memory and longing.

Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Hugstari as 'strategist, or the bold one'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Húsdrápa means 'house-lay': a drápa about the carved scenes on the panels of a hall.
Hvergelmir means 'bubbling boiling spring': hverr 'cauldron, hot spring' and gelmir 'roarer'.
The meaning of Hymir is uncertain; it may be related to Norwegian humen 'limp, weary' or humre 'whinny'.
Hyrrokkin is glossed 'fire-smoked', 'withered by fire': the giantess who launches Baldr's ship.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Iðavöllr possibly means 'splendour-plain' or 'green plain'.
Iði is glossed 'the moveable' or 'the hard-working one'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Iðunn has been explained as 'ever young', 'rejuvenator' or 'the rejuvenating one', fitting the apples that keep the gods young. It was also used as a woman's name in Iceland from the settlement onward.

means.en: lord of the friends of Ing

text.en: Ingunar-Freyr is a name of Freyr; Beowulf's close form frea Ingwina means 'lord of the friends of Ing'.
Ívaldi is glossed 'wielder of the yew bow' or 'warrior'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Járnsaxa means 'iron dagger' (járn 'iron', sax 'short sword').

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Járnviðr means 'iron wood': the forest east of Miðgarðr where the troll-women live.
Jörð is the ordinary word for 'earth'; she is the earth in person, Þórr's mother.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Jǫrmungandr is a poetic title. Jǫrmun- marks something huge, vast or superhuman, and some think of it as a noun for 'the world'. Gandr covers long things and supernatural beings: snake, staff, magic wand. Together they make roughly 'the huge (magic) beast'. He is also called Miðgarðsormr, 'the serpent of Miðgarðr'.
Jǫrmunrekkr is the Norse form of the Gothic king Ermanaric, *Airmanareiks: *ermena- 'universal, immense' and *-rīks 'ruler'. The first part is the same as in Jǫrmungandr.
Jórunn joins jǫfurr 'wild boar, prince' (Old English eofor) and unna 'to love'.

Jǫtunn, like Old English eoten and the archaic English ettin, goes back to Proto-Germanic *etunaz. Vladimir Orel thinks it likely related to *etanan 'to eat'. The giants are also called risi, þurs and troll, and giantesses gýgr.
Jǫtunheimar, usually in the plural in the Eddas, means 'giant-lands': jǫtunn 'giant' and heimr 'world, home'.
Kálfsvísa means 'Kálfr's vísa', perhaps after the name of its maker.

means.en: the wild, stormy one, or curl

text.en: Kára either means 'the wild, stormy one' (compare afkárr 'wild') or 'curl'.
Kári is glossed 'wind gust' or 'curly'; the giant is the wind itself.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Kerlaugar is the plural of kerlaug 'kettle-bath': the rivers Þórr wades each day.
Kíli is glossed 'wedge'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Kjárr comes from the title Caesar, through an early Germanic *kaisaraz; in the poems he is a king in the south, first of all the Roman emperor.
Kólga, one of Ægir's daughters (the waves), is glossed 'cool', from kaldr 'cold'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: The origin of Kvasir is uncertain. The root kvas- likely comes from Proto-Germanic *kvass- 'to squeeze, crush'; A. M. Sturtevant notes that juice comes from what is crushed (Danish kvase), which fits a being made from the gods' spittle and turned into mead.
The meaning of Læraðr is unclear: læ 'harm, betrayal' would give 'arranger of betrayal', while a reading *hléraðr 'giver of shelter' has also been suggested.
The meaning of Laufey is not clear; it is generally taken to be related to lauf 'leaves, foliage', perhaps 'the leafy one'. Her other name is Nál, 'needle'.
Leikn is glossed 'witch'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the horses of the Æsir reads Lettfeti as 'light-foot'. The names describe the horses' looks or gait; nothing more is told of them.
Litr means 'colour' or 'countenance, complexion': the dwarf Þórr kicks into Baldr's pyre.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: The meaning of Lóðurr is unknown. Links with lóð 'fruit, land', ljóðar 'people', laða 'to attract', Gothic liudan 'to grow' and German lodern 'to blaze' have all been suggested.
Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Lofarr as 'stooper'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Lofn possibly means 'comforter', 'the mild one' or 'loving'.
Logi means 'fire, flame': the fire itself, with whom Loki has to compete in eating at Útgarða-Loki's.

means.en: perhaps the one who closes or knots

text.en: The name Loki has been much debated. A link with logi 'flame' has no sound linguistic basis. Later Scandinavian forms (Danish Loke, Faroese Lokki, Swedish Locke) point to a Germanic root *luk- for loops, knots, hooks and locks; compare Faroese lokkanet 'cobweb', literally 'Lokki's net'. His other name Loptr is usually taken from lopt 'air'.
Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Lóni as 'lazy one'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Magni means 'strength', from megin 'might': Þórr's son, who will inherit the hammer.
Mánagarmr means 'moon-hound' or 'moon's dog': the wolf that swallows the moon.
Máni is the ordinary word for 'moon': the moon in person, Sól's brother.

Miðgarðr is 'the middle enclosure', from Common Germanic *meðjana-garðaz; the same word appears as Gothic midjungards, Old High German mittilagart and Old English middangeard, which became Middle English middellærd, 'Middle-earth'.

The most accepted explanation derives Mímir from a reduplicated form of Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- 'to think, recall, reflect' (Sanskrit smárati), so that the name is a distant relative of English memory. Rudolf Simek renders it 'the rememberer, the wise one'.
Mímisbrunnr means 'Mímir's wellspring'.
Mist means 'cloud' or 'mist'.
Mjöðvitnir is glossed 'mead-wolf', 'knowing in mead' or 'toper'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

means.en: lightning-maker, or the shining one, or the grinder

text.en: The meaning of Mjǫllnir is disputed. One proposal links it, through Proto-Norse *melluniaR, to Old Church Slavonic mlunuji and Russian molnija 'lightning', giving 'lightning-maker'; another to Old Norse mjǫll 'new snow' (Icelandic mjalli 'white'), giving 'shining (lightning) weapon'; a third to mala 'to grind' (Gothic malwjan), giving 'the grinder'.
Móði means 'wrath, courage', from móðr 'mood, wrath'. With his brother Magni 'strength' and his sister Þrúðr, he embodies his father Þórr's qualities, as Rudolf Simek notes.

Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Móðsognir as 'he who roars in rage'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Mögþrasir possibly means 'the one who is striving for sons'.

means.en: the one moving by fixed times

text.en: Mundilfari has been read as 'the one moving according to particular times', fitting the father of Sól and Máni; the meaning is not certain.

Muninn is munr with the definite ending. Munr covers affection, intent and will: 'care, urge, yearning, curiosity, memory'. It survives in Icelandic munur and is related to English mind and Old English gemynd 'memory'. Huginn and Muninn were probably near-synonyms for Óðinn's thought and memory.

The etymology of Múspell is uncertain. It may come from a compound meaning 'world-destroyers' or 'wreck of the world'; the word is also found in the Old High German poem Muspilli about the end of the world.
Myrkviðr means 'dark wood' or 'black forest'.
Naglfar means 'nail-farer': the ship made from the nails of the dead.
Naglfari is glossed 'nail-farer', like the ship Naglfar.

text.en: Náinn is glossed 'corpse', from nár 'corpse'.

means.en: mother, woman, or the daring one

text.en: The meaning of Nanna is debated: a babble word nanna 'mother', Jan de Vries's root *nanþ- 'the daring one', or, as John Lindow suggests, an Old Norse common noun for 'woman'.
Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Nár as 'corpse'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Narfi, also Nörfi, has been linked with Old Saxon narouua 'night' and with Old Norse nǫrr 'narrow'; as Adolf Noreen first suggested, the giant who is Night's father may simply be 'night'.
Nari is glossed 'corpse'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Náströnd means 'corpse shore': the hall in Hel where Níðhǫggr feeds on the dead.

means.en: the dark mountains, or mountains of the waning moon

text.en: Niðafjöll ends in fjǫll 'mountains, fells'; the first part is unclear, perhaps related to nið 'the waning moon', so 'mountains of waning'.

means.en: the striker below, or the striker in malice

text.en: -hǫggr means 'hewer, striker, biter'. The first part is unclear: niðr 'down' would give 'striker below (the roots)', níð 'shame, malice' would give 'malice-striker'.

text.en: Niði is glossed 'underworld being' or 'the one associated with the dark moon' (ný ok nið, new and waning moon).

text.en: Nifl 'mist' is related to Old English nifol 'dark, gloomy', Old High German nebul 'fog' and Greek nephélē 'cloud'; heimr is 'world, home'.
Niflhel means 'misty Hel': nifl 'mist, fog' and Hel.

text.en: Njörðr corresponds to Nerthus, the goddess Tacitus describes in the first century; both go back to Proto-Germanic *Nerþuz. The original meaning is contested; it may be related to Irish nert 'force, power'. Place names such as Njarðvík in Iceland keep his name.
Nóatún means 'ship-enclosure': nór 'ship' and tún 'enclosure, homestead'. It is Njörðr's home by the sea.
Norðri means 'northern, the one in the north'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Nóri is glossed 'little shaver'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: The origin of norn is uncertain. It may come from a word meaning 'to twine', for the thread of fate; Bek-Pedersen links it with the Swedish dialect verb norna 'to communicate secretly'.
Nótt is the ordinary word for 'night': the night in person.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of jötnar in Norse mythology

text.en: Óðinn goes back to Proto-Germanic *Wōðanaz, like Old English Wōden and Old High German Wuotan: the adjective *wōðaz 'possessed, inspired, raging' with a suffix meaning 'master of', so 'lord of frenzy' or 'leader of the possessed'. Old Norse óðr 'mad, furious' comes from the same word; Adam of Bremen glossed Wodan as Latin furor.
Óðr means 'mind, wit, soul, sense', or, as Andy Orchard gives it, 'the frenzied one'; it is the same word that lies behind Óðinn.
Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Óinn as 'shy'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

text.en: Óri is glossed 'the insane' or 'the violent one'.

text.en: Ótr means 'otter', the shape he takes when Loki kills him.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Óttarr is believed to come from ótti 'fear, dread'; it is the same name as Old English Ohthere.
Óttarr is believed to come from ótti 'fear, dread'; it is Old English Ohthere. Svarti, 'the black', is his byname.
Ráðsviðr is glossed 'powerful in advice, wise in counsel'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Ragnarr is built on the same first word as regin 'the ruling powers, the gods'.

The common noun rán means 'plundering, robbery', and the sea-goddess's name is read the same way. Rudolf Simek says the meaning is not fully clear, but she was probably understood as 'robber', and the name has nothing to do with ráða 'to rule'.

Ratatoskr is generally taken as 'drill-tooth' or 'bore-tooth': toskr 'tusk' and rata-, perhaps the same word as Rati, the drill Óðinn uses. Guðbrandur Vigfússon read it as 'tusk the traveller'; Sophus Bugge thought it borrowed from Old English 'rat-tooth'.
Regin has been glossed 'great, vast', 'the potent one' or 'the wielder'; compare regin 'the ruling powers, the gods'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Rekkr as 'warrior, hero, man'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Röskva comes from rǫskr 'fast, quick, brave, skilled'.
According to Guðbrandur Vigfússon, Róta is connected with róta 'sleet and storm', 'a goddess who sends storm and rain'.
The name Sæhrímnir is problematic. Modern scholarship commonly takes it as 'sooty sea-beast', though Snorri calls it a boar; it may be connected with seyðir 'cooking pit'.
Sága possibly means 'seeress'; it is related to the verb sjá 'to see'.
Saxland is 'the land of the Saxons' (saxar).
Sessrúmnir means 'seat-room', a hall with many seats: Freyja's hall.
Sif is the singular of sifjar 'relationship by marriage, kin', related to Old English sibb and English sib, and to German Sippe.
Sigrún means 'victory rune', from sigr 'victory' and rún 'secret, rune'.
Sigtryggr is glossed 'sure of victory, victory-true'; it is one of Óðinn's names.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of names of Odin

text.en: Sigurðr, like Sigvard and the German Siegfried, is a two-part Germanic name whose first part is *sigi- 'victory'.
Sigyn means '(woman) friend of victory': sigr 'victory' and vina 'friend'.
Wikipedia's article on the horses of the Æsir reads Silfrintoppr as 'silver-tuft'. The names describe the horses' looks or gait; nothing more is told of them.
Sindri comes from sindr 'slag, cinder': the smith dwarf.
Singasteinn means 'singing stone' or 'chanting stone'.
Wikipedia's article on the horses of the Æsir reads Sinir as 'sinewy'. The names describe the horses' looks or gait; nothing more is told of them.

Skaði may be related to Gothic skadus, Old English sceadu 'shadow'; John McKinnell notes that this could make her a personification of Scandinavia, whose name may contain hers, or link her with the underworld. Others connect the name with Old Norse words for 'harm'.
Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Skáfiðr as 'the scraper'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

means.en: the one that snorts as he runs

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the horses of the Æsir reads Skeidbrimir as 'the one that snorts as he runs'. The names describe the horses' looks or gait; nothing more is told of them.

means.en: assembled from thin pieces of wood

text.en: Skíðblaðnir is read as 'assembled from thin pieces of wood': skíð 'thin slip of wood' and blað 'leaf, blade'. It is Freyr's ship, which folds up like a cloth.
Skinfaxi means 'shining mane': Day's horse, whose mane lights up the sky and the earth.

Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Skirfir as 'skilful craftsman'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Skírnir means 'bright one', from skírr 'bright, pure'.
Skögul means 'shaker', or possibly 'high-towering'.
Sköll has been translated as 'treachery' or 'mockery'. It is a feminine form of skall 'bark, loud echoing sound', from the verb skjalla, skella 'to bark, to scold'; English scold is related.
Skuld means 'debt, obligation' and shares its origin with English should; it is often read as 'what shall be'.
Slagfiðr means 'beating-Finn'.
Sleipnir means 'slippy' or 'the slipper': the horse that glides.
Snotra means 'clever, wise': the goddess of wisdom.
Sökkvabekkr is glossed 'sunken bank', 'sunken bench' or 'treasure bank': Sága's home.
Sól is the ordinary word for 'sun': the sun in person. Old Norse also has the poetic synonym sunna, and the other Germanic languages call her Sunne or Sunna.
Suðri means 'southern, the one in the south'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Surtr means 'black', or more narrowly 'swart'. Surtsey, the volcanic island that rose off Iceland in 1963, is named after him.
Svaðilfari translates as 'the one making an unlucky journey' or 'unlucky traveller': the stallion that helped build the gods' wall.
Sváfa has been read as 'sleep-maker' or as 'Swabian' (Suebian).
Sváfnir is glossed 'sleep-bringer, closer'; it is one of Óðinn's names and also a serpent's.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of names of Odin

means.en: the home of the black elves

text.en: Svartálfaheimr is the home of the svartálfar, 'black elves', also called myrkálfar, 'dark elves'.
Svipdagr means 'sudden day'.

Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Svíurr as 'the disappearing one'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: Svíþjóð is 'the people of the Swedes' (svíar and þjóð 'people').
Tanngnjóstr means 'teeth-grinder, teeth-gnasher'; Rudolf Simek thinks the name may be Snorri's own.
Tanngrisnir means 'teeth-barer, snarler'. Rudolf Simek notes that the goats' names were young when recorded and may be Snorri's own.

Wikipedia's list of dwarfs in Norse mythology reads Þekkr as 'the welcome one, or beloved'. Most dwarf names in the lists are such descriptive words; for many the reading is a guess from the sound of the name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of dwarfs in Norse mythology

text.en: The etymology of Þjálfi is unclear; an origin in *þewa-alfaR 'serving-elf' has been proposed. The name was also used by real people: it is on more than a dozen Swedish runestones.
Þökk means 'thanks'; the giantess, presumed to be Loki in disguise, refuses to weep for Baldr.

Þórr is the Norse form of the thunder-god's name shared across Germanic: Old English Þunor, Old High German Donar, Old Saxon Thunar, from a Proto-Germanic name built on the word for thunder (*Þun(a)raz). The exact early form is debated. English Thursday is 'Þunor's day'.
Þorinn is glossed 'the daring, bold'. Tolkien took the name for Thorin Oakenshield.

text.en: Þrúðheimr means 'home of strength': Þórr's home.
Þrúðr means 'strength': Þórr's daughter, whose name matches her father's Þrúðvangr, 'plains of strength'.
Þrúðvangr (plural Þrúðvangar) means 'power-field, plains of strength': Þórr's land.
Þrymr is glossed 'uproar, noise'.

text.en: Týr comes from Proto-Germanic *Tīwaz, simply 'god' (Old English Tīw, Old High German Ziu), from Proto-Indo-European *deywós 'heavenly one', the word behind Latin deus and Sanskrit devá. In Old Norse poetry týr also means 'a god' and tívar 'the gods'; English Tuesday is Tīw's day.
There is no agreed origin for Tyrfing. It may be connected with the Thervingi, a Gothic tribe; another reading is 'Týr's finger'.

Ullr goes back to Proto-Germanic *Wulþuz 'glory', the same word as Gothic wulþus 'glory, wealth'. It comes from a Proto-Indo-European word for 'sight, appearance' and is an exact relative of Latin vultus 'face, expression'.
Uppsalir means 'upper halls, upper dwellings'.
Urðarbrunnr means 'well of Urðr', either the norn or urðr 'fate' itself.
Urðr means 'fate'; it is the same word as Old English wyrd.
Útgarða-Loki means 'Loki of the Outyards' or 'of the Outlands', to tell him from the Loki of the gods.
Útgarðar means 'outyards', the lands outside the enclosure, plural of Útgarðr.
Vafþrúðnir means 'mighty weaver' (of riddles), the wise giant whom Óðinn outwits.
Vakr is glossed 'wakeful, awakener'; it is one of Óðinn's names.

sources.title: Wikipedia: List of names of Odin

text.en: Valaskjálf is glossed 'the shelf of the slain': one of Óðinn's halls.

means.en: the hall (or rock) of the slain

text.en: Valhǫll joins valr 'the slain' (Old English wæl, as in valkyrie, 'chooser of the slain') and hǫll 'hall'. The second element may first have meant 'rock', so the name may once have been 'rock of the slain'. The English form Valhalla comes from an attempt to show the word's grammatical gender.
Valkyrja joins valr 'the slain' and kjósa 'to choose': 'chooser of the slain'. It is the same word as Old English wælcyrge.
Vanaheimr means 'home of the Vanir'.
Many etymologies have been proposed for Vanir. R. I. Page says it is tempting to link the word with Old Norse vinr 'friend' and Latin Venus. In English it is sometimes rendered Wanes.
Veðrfölnir means 'storm-pale', 'wind-bleached' or 'wind-witherer': the hawk between the eagle's eyes on Yggdrasill.
Verðandi is the present participle of verða 'to become', so 'in the making, that which is happening'; German werden 'to become' is the same verb.
Vestri means 'western, the one in the west'.

text.en: Vǫlsungr is 'the one of Völsi's kin', with the family ending -ung, as Old English Wælsing is from Wæls. The older name Völsi also appears in Vǫlsa þáttr, the story of a horse phallus that was worshipped.
Vǫluspá means 'the prophecy of the vǫlva', the seeress: vǫlva and spá 'prophecy'.
Vǫlundr goes back to Proto-Germanic *Wēlandaz, from *Wilą-ndz, literally 'crafting one'; the same smith is Wayland in English and Wieland in German.

means.en: Óðinn's horse, that is the gallows

text.en: The accepted meaning is 'Yggr's horse': drasill is 'horse' and Yggr 'the terrible one' is a name of Óðinn. 'The horse of the hanged' is a kenning for the gallows, so the name points to Óðinn hanging himself on the tree, as Hávamál tells.

Ymir goes back to a Proto-Indo-European word for 'twin' (*yemH-). He is a distant relative of Sanskrit Yama, the twin who was the first man to die, and has been compared with Remus, slain by his twin. The name fits a being from whom both sexes and all the giants came.
As a dwarf's name in Völuspá, Yngvi is glossed 'prince' or 'warrior'; it is also a name of Freyr.
